questions.stem: Which issue would be studied in microeconomics rather than macroeconomics?
options: Why the national unemployment rate rose over the past year
How fast the Australian economy as a whole is growing
What causes the general price level to keep rising
How a spring frost affects the price of Victorian apples
questions.explanation: Microeconomics studies individual markets, consumers and businesses, such as the market for apples. The national unemployment rate, total growth and the general price level are economy-wide aggregates, which are the subject of macroeconomics.

questions.stem: An economist studies how total spending by all Australian households affects the national unemployment rate. This is an example of:
options: microeconomics, because it studies one market for labour
macroeconomics, because it studies economy-wide aggregates
microeconomics, because it studies the decisions of households
normative economics, because it is concerned with unemployment
questions.explanation: Total household spending and the national unemployment rate describe the economy as a whole, so this is macroeconomics. Households are mentioned, but the study is of their combined spending, not of individual household decisions in one market.

questions.stem: Which statement is an example of positive economics?
options: Reducing smoking ought to be the government's top priority.
Raising the price of cigarettes will reduce the quantity smokers buy.
The government should tax cigarettes more heavily than alcohol.
It is unfair that low-income earners pay so much tax on their cigarettes.
questions.explanation: A positive statement is about what is, was or will be, and can be tested against evidence. The others use 'should', 'unfair' and 'ought', which signal value judgements, the mark of normative economics.

questions.stem: A newspaper column contains four statements about the minimum wage. Which one is normative?
options: After the minimum wage rose, some employers reduced workers' hours.
The minimum wage is reviewed each year by the Fair Work Commission.
Australia ought to raise the minimum wage to protect low-paid workers.
A higher minimum wage will raise the incomes of some low-paid workers.
questions.explanation: 'Ought to' expresses an opinion about what should happen, which makes the statement normative. The claim that a higher minimum wage raises some workers' incomes is positive, because it can be checked against data, even though it concerns a policy debate.

questions.stem: The statement 'Cutting income tax rates will reduce total tax revenue' is best described as:
options: normative, because it concerns a decision about government policy
positive, because economists generally agree that it is correct
positive, because it can be tested against evidence even if it proves false
normative, because economists disagree about whether it is true
questions.explanation: A positive statement makes a testable claim about cause and effect; it does not have to be true. Disagreement among economists, or a link to a policy decision, does not make a statement normative. Only a value judgement about what should happen does.

questions.stem: As a factor of production, capital refers to:
options: the money that a business borrows from a bank when it first starts operating
the natural resources, such as minerals and soil, found in a country
the physical and mental effort that people put into production
man-made goods, such as machinery, used to produce other goods and services
questions.explanation: In economics, capital is the stock of man-made resources, such as tools, machinery and buildings, used in production. Money borrowed is financial capital, which buys these resources but does not itself produce anything. Natural resources are land, and human effort is labour.

questions.stem: A Gippsland dairy farm uses pasture, milking machines and farmhands. As factors of production, these are respectively:
options: capital, land and labour
land, labour and capital
capital, capital and labour
land, capital and labour
questions.explanation: Pasture is a natural resource, so it is land; milking machines are man-made aids to production, so they are capital; farmhands supply labour. Pasture is sometimes mistaken for capital because the farmer improves it, but it remains a natural resource.

questions.stem: The basic economic problem of relative scarcity arises because:
options: needs and wants are unlimited but the resources to satisfy them are limited
some goods are produced in quantities that are too small to sell at a profit
resources are poorly managed by the governments of most economies
only poorer economies have too few resources to meet their needs
questions.explanation: Relative scarcity is the gap between unlimited needs and wants and the limited resources available to satisfy them. It faces every economy, rich or poor, which is why every society must make choices about how to use its resources.

questions.stem: Economists describe scarcity as 'relative' because:
options: scarcity affects some households but not others, depending on income
a good is scarce only when the market has completely run out of it
resources are limited compared with the wants they are needed to satisfy
some resources are scarcer in Australia than in other countries
questions.explanation: Scarcity is relative to wants: even plentiful resources are scarce if they cannot satisfy every want. Scarcity is not limited to low-income households or to empty shelves; a wealthy household still has to choose because its time and income are limited.

questions.stem: Mia has a free Saturday. She could work a café shift for $150, go to the beach or study. She chooses to study, and the beach was her second choice. Her opportunity cost is:
options: the $150 from the café shift
the café shift and the beach combined
the time she spends studying
the day at the beach
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up, and Mia ranked the beach second. The café wage is easy to measure in dollars, but it was not her next best choice, and opportunity cost counts only one alternative, not every option forgone.

questions.stem: The federal government spends $1 billion on a new defence project. The opportunity cost of this decision is:
options: the most valued alternative use of the funds, such as more hospital funding
the $1 billion itself, which is the amount paid for the defence project
every other project that the government could have funded with the $1 billion
the taxes the public must pay so that the defence project is funded
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the benefit of the single best alternative forgone, such as hospitals the money could have funded. The $1 billion is the money cost, not the opportunity cost, and opportunity cost is the next best alternative only, not every possible alternative.

questions.stem: An economy's PPF passes through these combinations of cars and computers: (0, 60), (10, 50), (20, 30) and (30, 0). Moving from 10 to 20 cars, the opportunity cost of each extra car is:
options: 20 computers
1 computer
3 computers
2 computers
questions.explanation: Moving from 10 to 20 cars cuts computer output from 50 to 30, so 10 extra cars cost 20 computers, or 2 computers per car. Twenty computers is the cost of all 10 cars, not of each one; the cost per car rises along the frontier, from 1 to 2 to 3 computers.

questions.stem: Josh could earn $200 working on Sunday or go to a concert whose ticket costs $90. Working is his next best alternative. The full economic cost to Josh of going to the concert is:
questions.explanation: The full cost of the concert is the money paid for the ticket plus the wage he gives up: $90 + $200 = $290. Counting only the $90 ticket ignores the opportunity cost of not working, which a cost-benefit analysis must include.

questions.stem: A point inside an economy's production possibility frontier shows that:
options: some resources are unemployed or under-utilised
the economy is producing at its most efficient level
the combination cannot be produced with current resources
the economy has recently experienced economic growth
questions.explanation: Inside the frontier, the economy could produce more of one or both goods by putting idle resources to work, so resources are under-utilised. A point outside the frontier, not inside it, is unattainable with current resources and technology.

questions.stem: Which event would shift Australia's production possibility frontier outwards?
options: a fall in the price of the goods that Australia exports
a new technology that raises the output of each worker
a fall in unemployment as idle workers find new jobs
a shift of resources from producing services to goods
questions.explanation: Better technology raises what the economy can produce with its resources, so the whole frontier moves out. Putting idle workers to work moves the economy from inside the frontier towards it, but does not move the frontier itself.

questions.stem: During a recovery, an economy moves from a point inside its production possibility frontier to a point on it. Which statement is correct?
options: The frontier itself has shifted outwards to a new position
More of one good can be produced only by giving up the other
The economy must have gained new resources or technology
More of both goods can be produced without any opportunity cost
questions.explanation: Inside the frontier, resources are idle, so using them adds output of both goods without sacrificing either. A trade-off between the goods applies only once the economy is on the frontier, and the frontier shifts only when resources or technology change.

questions.stem: Why is a production possibility frontier usually drawn bowed outwards from the origin?
options: an economy always has some resources that are left unemployed
producing more of both goods becomes easier as total output grows
the prices of both goods rise as more of each one is produced
resources are not equally suited to both goods, so opportunity cost rises
questions.explanation: As an economy makes more of one good it must draw in resources less suited to it, so each extra unit costs more of the other good. A straight-line frontier would mean a constant opportunity cost. Unemployed resources are shown by a point inside the frontier, not by its shape.

questions.stem: In economics, a trade-off occurs when:
options: a business replaces one input with a cheaper input at no cost
choosing more of one thing means accepting less of something else
two parties voluntarily exchange goods for money in a market transaction
a cost is shared equally between the buyers and the sellers
questions.explanation: Because resources are scarce, getting more of one thing means giving up some of another: a trade-off. The value of what is given up is the opportunity cost. An exchange in a market is a transaction, not a trade-off.

questions.stem: A council uses cost-benefit analysis to decide whether to build a new bypass. Which approach is most consistent with this method?
options: build the bypass if its construction cost fits within the council's annual budget
build the bypass if a majority of the residents surveyed say that they would use it regularly
compare the bypass only with the cheapest alternative project that is available
weigh the bypass's expected benefits against all its costs, including opportunities forgone
questions.explanation: Cost-benefit analysis compares all the benefits of a decision with all its costs, including the opportunity cost of what else the money and land could do. A project can fit the budget and still cost more than it is worth, so affordability alone is not the test.

questions.stem: The three basic economic questions are:
options: how much to charge, how much to save, and how much to tax
what to consume, what to import, and what to export overseas
what and how much to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce
what to produce, where to produce it, and when to produce it
questions.explanation: Every economy must decide what and how much to produce, how to produce it, and who receives the output. Questions about location, timing, saving or trade are decisions that sit inside these three, not separate basic questions.

questions.stem: A supermarket decides whether to replace checkout staff with self-service machines. This addresses which basic economic question?
options: how to produce
what and how much to produce
for whom to produce
where to produce
questions.explanation: Choosing between labour and capital is a decision about the method of production, so it answers how to produce. The supermarket is still selling the same goods to the same customers, so what and for whom are unchanged.

questions.stem: A government raises unemployment payments, funded by higher taxes on high-income earners. Which basic economic question is it mainly addressing?
options: how much to produce, as it raises the total output produced
for whom to produce, as it changes who can buy the output
how to produce, as it changes how labour combines with capital
what to produce, as it changes the mix of goods that is made
questions.explanation: Redistributing income changes who has the purchasing power to receive goods and services, which is the question of for whom to produce. It does not directly change the method of production or the total amount the economy can produce.

questions.stem: In a market economy, the three basic economic questions are answered mainly by:
options: a central planning authority that sets output targets for each firm
custom and tradition handed down from one generation to the next
elected governments that own and run most businesses in the economy
the decisions of consumers and businesses, through the price mechanism
questions.explanation: In a market economy, consumers and businesses interact in markets, and prices signal what to produce and how. A central planning authority answers the questions in a planned economy, and custom answers them in a traditional economy.

questions.stem: Australia is best described as a mixed economy because:
options: it exports a broad mix of agricultural, mining and service products to the rest of the world
half its businesses are owned by government and half are owned privately
its economy is planned by government, with some private trade allowed
markets allocate most resources, but government also provides services and regulates
questions.explanation: Australia relies mainly on markets, but government provides services such as public schools and hospitals, redistributes income and regulates markets. A mixed economy is about who allocates resources, not the mix of exports, and government owns far less than half of businesses.

questions.stem: In a traditional economic system, how goods are produced and shared is decided mainly by:
options: prices that adjust to balance demand and supply in markets
a central government agency that sets production quotas
a vote of all citizens at regular national elections
custom, culture and practices passed down over generations
questions.explanation: Traditional economies answer the basic economic questions through custom and long-standing practice, such as which family members hunt or farm. Prices answer them in a market economy and a central agency in a planned economy.

questions.stem: Which is a key advantage claimed for market economies over planned economies?
options: income is shared out equally, so every household can afford the same range of goods
the government decides output, so shortages and surpluses cannot occur
businesses do not compete, so resources are not wasted on duplication
prices signal what consumers value, so resources flow to the goods most wanted
questions.explanation: In a market economy, changes in prices and profits signal where resources are most valued and draw resources there. Markets do not share income equally; a fair distribution is a common criticism of them, and planned economies are prone to shortages and surpluses.

questions.stem: In the three-sector circular flow model, households provide businesses with:
options: taxes in return for public goods
transfer payments such as pensions
factors of production such as labour
goods and services in return for income
questions.explanation: Households own the factors of production and supply them, mainly labour, to businesses in return for income such as wages. Goods and services flow the other way, from businesses to households.

questions.stem: In the three-sector circular flow model, which flow goes from government to households?
options: transfer payments, such as the age pension
income tax deducted from workers' wages
wages paid by private businesses for labour
consumption spending on goods and services
questions.explanation: Government pays transfers such as pensions and unemployment payments to households, and provides public goods and services. Income tax flows the other way, from households to government; wages and consumption spending pass between households and businesses.

questions.stem: In the three-sector circular flow model, the government raises income tax rates while leaving its spending unchanged. The most likely immediate effect is:
options: a rise in the flow of income paid by businesses to their workers
a rise in household spending as government revenue increases
a fall in tax revenue as the government spends less on households
a fall in household spending, slowing the flow of income to businesses
questions.explanation: Higher income tax leaves households with less disposable income, so they spend less, and businesses receive less revenue. Government revenue rises, but because its spending is unchanged, that extra revenue is not returned to the flow.

questions.stem: The main purpose of economic activity is to:
options: satisfy needs and wants and so improve living standards
maximise the profits that businesses earn in the economy
raise the tax revenue that the government collects each year
increase the amount of money circulating in the economy
questions.explanation: People produce, distribute and consume goods and services to satisfy their needs and wants, which raises living standards. Profits and tax revenue are outcomes of economic activity, not its purpose.

questions.stem: Which change is mainly an improvement in non-material living standards?
options: more households owning a car and a computer
a rise in the quantity of goods each person buys
less traffic congestion, shortening daily commutes
a rise in average household disposable income
questions.explanation: Non-material living standards are the qualitative parts of wellbeing, such as time, health and the environment, so shorter commutes improve them. Incomes and the goods households own or buy measure material living standards.

questions.stem: The public sector of the Australian economy consists of:
options: companies that sell their shares to members of the public on the stock exchange
all households and consumers who buy goods and services in the economy
businesses owned by individuals or by groups of private shareholders
organisations owned or controlled by government, such as public hospitals
questions.explanation: The public sector is the part of the economy owned or controlled by government at any level. A company listed on the stock exchange is a 'public company', but it is privately owned by its shareholders, so it belongs to the private sector.

questions.stem: The traditional economic viewpoint assumes that consumers:
options: choose the cheapest product regardless of the satisfaction it gives
act rationally in their own self-interest to maximise their utility
make most choices based mainly on habit, emotion and impulse
aim to maximise the wellbeing of the whole community over their own
questions.explanation: The traditional view sees consumers as rational, self-interested and informed, choosing the combination of goods that maximises their utility. Habit and emotion are departures from that model studied by behavioural economics.

questions.stem: Ella eats slices of pizza. The first slice gives her the most satisfaction and each further slice gives her less. This illustrates:
options: bounded willpower in consumer decision-making
diminishing marginal benefit from consumption
rising opportunity cost of producing pizza
the law of supply in the market for pizza
questions.explanation: The extra satisfaction, or marginal benefit, from each additional unit falls as more is consumed. Bounded willpower would be Ella eating more than she knows is good for her, which is not what is described.

questions.stem: In the traditional view, a rational consumer will keep buying extra units of a good as long as:
options: the price of the good stays below the average price of other goods
the marginal benefit of each unit keeps rising as more are bought
the marginal benefit of the next unit is at least equal to its price
the total benefit of all the units bought remains greater than zero
questions.explanation: A rational consumer compares the extra benefit of one more unit with its extra cost, the price, and stops once the marginal benefit falls below the price. Total benefit can stay positive long after the last unit is no longer worth buying.

questions.stem: The government offers a $3,000 rebate to households that install a home battery. In traditional economic theory, the rebate is expected to:
options: lower the number of batteries installed, as the price of batteries rises
affect only the businesses that manufacture and sell home batteries
act as an incentive, raising the number of households installing batteries
act as a disincentive, as households must pay before claiming the rebate
questions.explanation: A rebate lowers the effective cost of a battery, so more households find that its benefits exceed its cost. Paying up front and claiming later still leaves the household better off than without the rebate, so it remains an incentive.

questions.stem: A cut in the marginal income tax rate for middle-income earners is most likely to act as:
options: a disincentive to work longer hours, as workers pay less tax on each extra dollar that they earn
an incentive to work fewer hours, as take-home pay for each extra hour of work falls
a disincentive to spend, as households are required to save their extra income
an incentive for some workers to work extra hours, as they keep more of each extra dollar
questions.explanation: A lower marginal tax rate raises the after-tax reward for each extra hour worked, an incentive to work more. Take-home pay per hour rises, not falls, when the marginal rate is cut.

questions.stem: A state government increases the fines for using a mobile phone while driving. This is an example of:
options: a tax that raises the cost of buying a mobile phone
a regulation creating a disincentive for a behaviour
a subsidy creating an incentive for safer driving
a tax rebate rewarding drivers who obey road rules
questions.explanation: A road rule backed by a fine is a regulation, and a larger fine raises the expected cost of breaking it, a disincentive. A fine is not a tax on buying phones; it applies only to the behaviour the rule forbids.

questions.stem: In the traditional economic viewpoint, the main objective of a business is to:
options: maximise its profit
maximise its workers' wages
maximise the community's welfare
minimise the taxes it pays
questions.explanation: The traditional view assumes businesses aim to maximise profit, the difference between revenue and costs. Businesses may pursue other goals, but profit maximisation is the assumption of the traditional model.

questions.stem: The government places a tax on each tonne of carbon dioxide that factories emit. A profit-maximising factory is most likely to respond by:
options: ignoring the tax, since the factory's customers are the ones who pay it
raising its emissions so that it qualifies for a larger tax rebate
investing in cleaner technology if this costs less than paying the tax
producing more output to spread the tax across more units of output
questions.explanation: The tax adds a cost to every tonne emitted, so a profit-maximising firm will cut emissions wherever doing so is cheaper than paying. Producing more would raise emissions and the tax bill, not spread it, because the tax is per tonne emitted.

questions.stem: The government pays employers a subsidy for each apprentice they hire. A business is most likely to respond by:
options: hiring fewer apprentices, as the subsidy raises the wages they must be paid
raising its prices, as the subsidy increases the business's total costs
replacing apprentices with machinery, as labour is now more expensive
hiring more apprentices, as the subsidy lowers the cost of employing them
questions.explanation: A subsidy paid to the employer lowers the net cost of hiring an apprentice, an incentive to hire more. It does not raise the business's costs; it reduces them.

questions.stem: In the traditional economic viewpoint, the main aim of government in the economy is to:
options: maximise the profits of local businesses
maximise the tax revenue it collects
minimise the size of the private sector
maximise the living standards of society
questions.explanation: The traditional view sees government acting to maximise society's living standards. Tax revenue is a means of funding that aim, not the aim itself.

questions.stem: A progressive income tax combined with means-tested family payments mainly serves which role of government?
options: maximising the profits earned by private businesses
redistributing income to improve living standards
improving efficiency by correcting pollution problems
stabilising prices by lowering the rate of inflation
questions.explanation: Taxing higher incomes at higher rates and paying benefits to lower-income families moves income from those with more to those with less, which is redistribution. Neither tool is aimed at pollution or at lowering inflation.

questions.stem: The government taxes sugary drinks, whose overconsumption imposes health costs that fall partly on the public health system. This mainly reflects its role of:
options: redistributing income from high to low earners
stabilising the overall level of economic activity
maximising the profits of drink manufacturers
improving efficiency in the allocation of resources
questions.explanation: When a good imposes costs on others that buyers ignore, the market overproduces it, and a tax moves resources towards a more efficient allocation. The tax targets that misallocation of resources rather than moving income from high earners to low earners.

questions.stem: When the government increases its spending during a recession to support jobs, it is mainly performing its role of:
options: economic stabilisation
redistribution of income
efficient resource allocation
profit maximisation
questions.explanation: Raising spending in a downturn smooths the business cycle, supporting output and employment, which is the stabilisation role. Redistribution concerns who receives income, not the overall level of activity.
